author: high
claim: In a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every trail having the maximum possible number of edges is closed.
evidence: Let the trail begin at s and end at t. If s and t are distinct, then in the subgraph formed by the trail edges, every intermediate visit to t uses one entering and one leaving edge, while the final visit contributes one extra entering edge; hence the number of used trail edges incident with t is odd. The ambient degree of t is even, so at least one incident edge is unused. Appending that edge at t gives a longer trail, contradicting maximality. Thus s=t.

links.statement: Any maximum-length trail in a finite even-degree undirected graph is closed.

author: high
claim: If a closed trail in a connected graph with at least one edge omits an edge, and every vertex of the graph has even degree, then there is a strictly longer trail.
evidence: Connectedness gives an omitted edge incident with a vertex v on the closed trail: take a path from a trail vertex to an endpoint of any omitted edge and choose the first path edge not on the trail. Remove all trail edges. At each vertex the closed trail used an even number of incident edges (each occurrence enters and leaves, including the cyclic junction), so every residual degree is even. The residual graph has an edge at v. A maximum-length residual trail starting at v is therefore nonempty and must end at v by the same endpoint-parity argument. Insert this residual closed trail into the original closed trail at v. The two edge sets are disjoint, so the result is a trail with more edges.

links.statement: An edge-omitting closed trail in the stated graph can be extended by residual-trail splicing.

glossary.v: a vertex lying on the original closed trail and incident with an omitted edge

author: high7
claim: A trail of maximum length in a finite connected undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree is closed and contains every edge.
evidence: Let T=(v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_m,v_m) be a trail with the maximum possible number of edges. Such a trail exists because the graph has finitely many edges. If v_0 != v_m, then among the used edges the degree of v_m is odd: every arrival at v_m before the last is paired with a departure, while the final arrival is unpaired (a loop contributes one arrival and one departure, so this remains valid). The degree of v_m in the whole graph is even, hence at least one incident edge is unused; appending it makes a longer trail, a contradiction. Thus T is closed. If an edge is unused, connectedness gives an unused edge incident to a vertex w occurring on T: if an endpoint of the unused edge is not already on T, follow a path from it to a vertex on T and take the first edge by which the path enters the vertex set of T. Cyclically rotate the closed trail T to begin and end at that occurrence of w, then append this unused incident edge. Again one obtains a longer trail, a contradiction. Therefore T is closed and traverses every edge exactly once.

links.statement: A trail of maximum length in a finite connected undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree is closed and contains every edge.

glossary.T: a trail having the maximum possible number of edges
glossary.v_i: the vertex at position i in the vertex-edge sequence of T
glossary.e_i: the edge at position i in the vertex-edge sequence of T
glossary.m: the number of edges of T
glossary.w: a vertex occurring on T and incident to an edge not used by T

author: high2
claim: In a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every edge-maximal trail that begins at a vertex a must end at a; moreover, deleting the edges of any closed trail leaves every residual vertex degree even.
evidence: Let a trail start at a and end at b. If b is different from a, the trail uses an odd number of edges incident with b: each earlier arrival at b is paired with a departure, while the final arrival is unpaired. Since the total degree of b is even, the number of unused incident edges is a nonnegative odd integer, hence positive, so the trail can be extended at b, contrary to edge-maximality. Thus b=a. For a closed trail, at every vertex each arrival is paired with a departure, so the trail uses an even number of incident edges there. Subtracting this even number from the original even degree leaves an even residual degree.

links.statement: Maximal trails close, and removal of a closed trail preserves even residual degrees.

glossary.a: the initial vertex of the trail
glossary.b: the terminal vertex of the trail

author: high5
claim: If G is a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, then every longest trail T in G is closed.
evidence: Write T from initial vertex v_0 to terminal vertex v_m and let H be the spanning subgraph whose edge set consists of the edges used by T. If v_m differs from v_0, the incidences at v_m contributed by T pair at every intermediate visit, with one unpaired final-arrival incidence, so deg_H(v_m) is odd. Longestness says that no edge outside T is incident with v_m, since such an edge could be appended. Hence deg_G(v_m)=deg_H(v_m), contradicting that deg_G(v_m) is even. Therefore v_m=v_0.

links.statement: Every longest trail in a finite even-degree undirected graph is closed.

glossary.G: the finite undirected graph under consideration
glossary.T: a trail of maximum possible number of edges in G
glossary.H: the subgraph consisting of all edges traversed by T together with their endpoints

author: high5
claim: If G is connected and a closed trail T omits an edge of G, then the cyclic order of T can be rotated and an omitted edge appended to obtain a strictly longer trail.
evidence: Let S be the vertices occurring on T. If an omitted edge already has an endpoint in S, use it. Otherwise, connectivity gives a path from S to an endpoint of an omitted edge, and the first edge of that path leaving S is omitted and incident with S. Call such an edge f and its endpoint on T w. Because T is closed, rotate its vertex-edge sequence to start and end at an occurrence of w; appending f then gives a trail using all edges of T once and f once, hence one more edge.

links.statement: Any non-edge-covering closed trail in a connected graph extends after cyclic rotation.

glossary.G: the connected undirected graph under consideration
glossary.S: the set of vertices occurring on T
glossary.f: an edge of G omitted by T and incident with a vertex of T
glossary.w: an endpoint of f that occurs on T

author: high6
claim: In any finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every trail having the maximum possible number of edges is closed.
evidence: Let T=(v_0,e_1,v_1,...,e_m,v_m) be a longest trail. Suppose v_0 and v_m are distinct. Let A be the number of indices i in {1,...,m} with v_i=v_m (arrivals at v_m), and let D be the number of indices i in {1,...,m} with v_{i-1}=v_m (departures from v_m). Since the sequence starts somewhere other than v_m and ends at v_m, A=D+1. The degree of v_m in the subgraph whose edges are e_1,...,e_m is A+D=2D+1, hence odd. Its degree in the whole graph is even, so not all edges incident with v_m occur in T. Appending an unused incident edge to T produces a longer trail, a contradiction. Therefore v_0=v_m. author: high3
claim: A longest trail in the given graph is closed and traverses every edge; hence it is the required Eulerian circuit.
evidence: Let T be a trail using as many edges as possible. Write it from initial vertex a to terminal vertex b. If a and b are distinct, then at b the incidences contributed by edges of T consist of pairs from every intermediate arrival/departure and one unpaired final arrival, so their number is odd. Since the degree of b in G is even, at least one edge incident with b is absent from T; appending it contradicts maximality. Thus T is closed. If T omits an edge, connectedness gives a vertex v occurring on T that is incident with an omitted edge: connect an endpoint of any omitted edge to the nonempty vertex set of T and take the first edge of the connecting path that enters that set (or use the omitted edge itself if its endpoint is already on T). Let R consist of all edges omitted by T. At each vertex, the T-edge incidences occur in arrival/departure pairs because T is closed, so the degree in R is even. Choose, among trails using only R and beginning at v, one Q with as many edges as possible; Q has at least one edge. If its terminal vertex differed from v, the same odd-incidence argument within R would provide another unused R-edge at that terminal vertex, contradicting maximality of Q. Hence Q is closed at v. Insert Q into T at an occurrence of v. The resulting closed trail uses all edges of T and Q without repetition and is strictly longer than T, contradiction. Therefore T omits no edge.

links.statement: A finite connected undirected graph with at least one edge and even degree at every vertex has a closed trail traversing every edge exactly once.

glossary.G: the finite connected undirected graph in the problem
glossary.T: a trail in G having the maximum possible number of edges
glossary.v: a vertex of T incident with an edge omitted by T
glossary.R: the set of edges of G omitted by T
glossary.Q: a longest trail using only edges in R and beginning at v

author: high4
claim: In a finite undirected graph in which every vertex has even degree, every trail of maximum possible length among trails starting at a fixed positive-degree vertex ends where it starts.
evidence: Let the trail start at s and end at t. If t differs from s, count incidences of its used edges at t. Every internal visit to t contributes two used incidences and the final arrival contributes one, so the number of used incidences at t is odd. The total degree of t is even, hence the number of unused incidences at t is a positive odd number. Thus an unused edge incident to t can be appended, contradicting maximal length. Therefore t=s.

links.statement: A maximal trail from a positive-degree vertex in a finite even-degree graph is closed.

glossary.t: the ending vertex of the chosen trail
